name: Pyongyang Grand Theatre
funding: State theatre, main stage of the Pibada (Sea of Blood) Opera Troupe, paid from the state budget. It reopened on 3 April 2009 after rebuilding (Korean Wikipedia).
watch: Opened 13 August 1960 with 2,190 seats. North Korean media reported about 1,300 seats after the 2009 rebuild.
why_flagged: State theatre, main stage of the Pibada (Sea of Blood) Opera Troupe, paid from the state budget. It reopened on 3 April 2009 after rebuilding (Korean Wikipedia).
affiliations_note: Home of the Pibada Opera Troupe, founded in 1946 as the North Korean Opera Troupe and renamed in 1971. The five revolutionary operas are staged here (Korean Wikipedia).

overview: Theatre at the junction of Yonggwang and Sungri streets in central Pyongyang, about 1 km south of Kim Il Sung Square and opposite the Pyongyang Hotel (Koryo Tours). The Korean Art website places it in Othan-dong, Central District.

Building began in February 1959 and finished on 13 August 1960. The site covers 75,000 square metres, with about 29,000 square metres of floor space over three floors and 2,190 seats at opening (Korean Wikipedia).
Koryo Tours calls it the first major Korean-style project completed in the rebuilt city, after years of Soviet-influenced buildings.
It is the home stage of the Pibada (Sea of Blood) Opera Troupe, where the five revolutionary operas are staged (Korean Wikipedia; Korean Art website).

Rebuilt from June 2008 and reopened on 3 April 2009. The 26th April Spring Friendship Art Festival was held there on 15 April to mark the opening. North Korean media reported about 1,300 seats afterwards (Korean Wikipedia). The Korean Art website lists a 1,262-seat auditorium, a 600-seat conference hall, a rotating stage, a polyclinic, a nursery school, a restaurant and a shop.

Visiting: Koryo Tours says foreign tourists seldom go inside, because the operas are not scheduled regularly or announced far ahead. The exterior is a common photo stop, and the restaurant inside is sometimes open to foreign visitors.
details.funding_verdict: Pyongyang Grand Theatre: state-run: the Government of North Korea
funding: The Ministry of Culture's Korean Art website lists the theatre as the home theatre of the Pibada Opera Troupe (archived copy).

North Korea announces its state budget as yearly percentage changes, not amounts. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5 percent of 2025 and spending 105.8 percent, with funds for the cultural sector at 103.1 percent of last year's and 15.8 percent of spending going to national defence.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions, state theatre
points: The theatre hosts the five revolutionary operas, other performances, and political and cultural events such as the April Spring Friendship Art Festival (Korean Art website).

not_related: the East Pyongyang Grand Theatre, a different theatre in the Taedonggang District, built in 1989 and used mainly by the Mansudae Art Troupe (Korean Wikipedia).
details.bottom_line: Pyongyang Grand Theatre is paid for by the North Korean state. The rebuilding in 2008 and 2009 and its use for the state's five operas are the points to watch.

sources.note: copy of a KCNA text; state media

name: Sinchon Museum of American War Atrocities
watch: A larger building opened in July 2015; closed to foreign visitors since 2018. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: The museum is dedicated to the Sinchon Massacre and exhibits the deaths of over 35,000 people from 17 October to 7 December 1950. It blames South Korean and US troops. Other research says Communists and anti-Communist vigilantes both killed civilians.

propaganda.summary: The museum presents North Korea's account that US troops killed over 35,000 people at Sinchon in 1950. Schools, army units and factories are sent on visits. Historian Adam Cathcart says the account underpinned anti-US propaganda.

overview: War museum in Sinchon County, South Hwanghae Province, reached on a day trip from Pyongyang (Jeppesen), dedicated to the Sinchon massacre of October to December 1950 (Wikipedia; Daily Beast).
Established on 26 March 1958. Rebuilt and moved to a new site in July 2015 (Wikipedia).
Named for Sinchon, the county where the killings took place. It attributes them to US and South Korean forces (Wikipedia).

What is on show: remains, belongings, images and paintings. The grounds include a grave of 400 mothers and children killed in the area (Wikipedia). A visitor writing in 2013 counted about a dozen rooms with survivor testimony, victim counts by district, paintings and photographs of bodies (Patrick Tapy, Sino-NK).
The museum shows a toll of over 35,000 dead between 17 October and 7 December 1950 (Wikipedia). The Korean Central News Agency gave 35,383 in 1998 (Wikipedia, Sinchon Massacre).
Visiting: the site is rarely on group itineraries for foreigners. Nearly every North Korean visits at least once on a mandatory educational trip (Travis Jeppesen, Daily Beast, 2018).
details.funding_verdict: Sinchon Museum of American War Atrocities: owner and funder not named in any page opened
funding: Adam Cathcart wrote in July 2015 that North Korea "has pumped significant resources into a refurbished museum in Sinchon"; he named no ministry, party body or other owner and gave no figure.
Wikipedia reports a Kim Jong Un visit in 2014 and that the museum was rebuilt and moved in July 2015; it names no owner.
wider_context: Historians outside North Korea dispute the museum's account. The Institute for Korean Historical Studies (South Korea) concluded that both communists and anti-communist vigilantes carried out killings, and that the 19th Infantry Regiment did not take part but failed to stop the South Korean secret police (Wikipedia).

Novelist Hwang Sok-yong attributes the massacre to local rivalry that used the chaos of war as cover (Wikipedia). Cathcart reports that the historian Bruce Cumings said he found nothing in the archives about a US occupation of Sinchon.

Adam Cathcart (University of Leeds), 19 July 2015: he found no evidence that an American unit entered Sinchon, and wrote that "no serious writing outside of North Korea has been made to determine if the body count is accurate"; he did not reach a firm conclusion on who did the killings.

Patrick Tapy (Sino-NK, 17 September 2013) says the visit gave "the impression of complete and unquestionable US guilt being used as a propaganda tool", and that North Korean historians "do not possess any more evidence of actual US responsibility" than independent scholars such as Bruce Cumings or Hwang Sok-yong.

A 1952 report by the International Association of Democratic Lawyers, prepared in Pyongyang, accused US forces; it relied on North Korean oral testimony (Wikipedia). No independent international investigation is described.
The death toll and the attribution to US forces are the museum's own claims.
details.bottom_line: The weak points are the lack of any published ownership, budget or board, and an official account of the killings and the toll that outside historians dispute and that nobody outside the state has been able to verify. Watch for any independent access to the site or archives.

name: South Hamgyong Sci-Tech Library
funding: State science and technology library for South Hamgyong Province; state media reported its opening ceremony in December 2018.
watch: Wikipedia dates the building to 2016 from Google Earth imagery. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: State science and technology library for South Hamgyong Province; state media reported its opening ceremony in December 2018.
affiliations_note: Provincial library of South Hamgyong Province, built on the site of the former South Hamgyong Cultural Exhibition House.

overview: Science and technology library in the centre of Hamhung, South Hamgyong Province.
Unverified: Wikipedia, citing NK News, says it is the first large-scale science and technology library outside Pyongyang.
NK News reported on 31 December 2018, citing state media, that an opening ceremony had been held the previous Sunday, more than two years after the project first appeared nearly complete.
Wikipedia says Google Earth imagery shows the building went up on the site of the former South Hamgyong Cultural Exhibition House between February and November 2016.
Wikipedia describes a mix of the architectural styles of Ryomyong New Town and Mirae Scientists Street, with two roof features resembling stylised hydrogen atoms and a helium atom statue in front.
details.funding_verdict: South Hamgyong Sci-Tech Library (Hamhung): state-run: a provincial science and technology library of the North Korean state
funding: NK News's account of the opening rests on state media.

The state announces its budget only as yearly percentage changes. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5% of 2025 and spending 105.8%, with funds for science and technology at 105.3% of last year's and for the cultural sector at 103.1%.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions, state body
points: Executive Order 13722 of 15 March 2016 blocks property of the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea that is in the United States or in the control of US persons (Federal Register, 18 March 2016). The library is a state body, and the order does not name it.

press.overall: One news report discusses the library: NK News on its opening in 2018.

items.title: Colin Zwirko, "New North Korean Sci-Tech Library officially opens after long delay" (2018)
points: Reports that state media announced an opening ceremony in Hamhung more than two years after the project first appeared nearly complete.
Notes that the facade shown in the state reports is nearly identical to a version aired earlier on state television.
Only the opening paragraphs were read.

details.bottom_line: The library is paid for by the North Korean state. The Sanctions basis is the weak point: the Government of North Korea is blocked under Executive Order 13722. Worth watching: the gap of more than two years between the building appearing nearly complete in 2016 and the announced opening in 2018.

sources.note: copy of a KCNA text; state media

name: Victorious Fatherland Liberation War Museum
funding: Opened 1953; moved to Sosong in 1963 per Koryo Tours, rebuilt 1974 per Korean Wikipedia. Shows the USS Pueblo.
watch: The ship, seized in 1968, is still on the US Navy commissioned roster. The Government of North Korea is blocked under US Executive Order 13722.
why_flagged: Opened 1953; moved to Sosong in 1963 per Koryo Tours, rebuilt 1974 per Korean Wikipedia. Shows the USS Pueblo. KCNA claimed nearly 800,000 visitors in 2014.
records_note: It is a state institution, and North Korea reports its state budget only as yearly percentage changes (spending up 3.8 percent in 2025, per the Korea Institute for National Unification).
affiliations_note: Runs the display of the USS Pueblo, moored beside it on the Botong River since 2013.

propaganda.summary: Founded 1953 and rebuilt 2013, when Kim Jong Un cut the ribbon. KCNA quoted Kim calling it a centre for anti-US and class education honouring Kim Il Sung's wartime victory over the United States.

overview: State museum of the Korean War in the Sosong District of Pyongyang, beside the Pothong River (Koryo Tours).
Set up in August 1953 in the Central District as the Fatherland Liberation War Museum. Korean Wikipedia gives 17 August 1953.
A new building opened next to the old one on 27 July 2013, the 60th anniversary of the armistice, and took in the old panorama (Koryo Tours). Lonely Planet also dates the current home to 2013.

KCNA said on 27 July 2014 that the museum was remodelled the year before, and claimed Kim Jong Un gave on-site guidance on 18 occasions. English Wikipedia dates the renovation to 2014 and cites that KCNA item.
The top-floor 360-degree display of the Battle of Taejon was upgraded in 2018 (Koryo Tours).
Outdoors are a War Victory Monument, an Exhibition of Hero Equipment and an Exhibition of Captured Equipment with US armoured vehicles, artillery, aircraft and a seaborne drone (Koryo Tours).

USS Pueblo, seized in January 1968, was moved from the Taedong River to the Pothong River beside the museum in late 2012 and opened to tourists in July 2013 (Wikipedia). It remains on the US Navy's commissioned list (Wikipedia, Koryo Tours).

Visiting: Koryo Tours says tourists and locals can visit with a guide in military uniform. A visit takes about two hours, after a security check. Photography is banned inside and allowed outside. The site is reached by car, bus or taxi.
details.funding_verdict: Victorious Fatherland Liberation War Museum: state-funded: the Government of North Korea
funding: Source conflict on the move to the Sosong District: Koryo Tours and the text of English Wikipedia say April 1963; korea-dpr.com (the Korean Friendship Association's site), Korean Wikipedia (11 April 1974) and the infobox of English Wikipedia say April 1974. Koryo Tours' page on the old museum says that building, next to the 2013 one, was completed in 1974.

North Korea announces its state budget as yearly percentage changes, not amounts. KCNA claimed on 24 March 2026 that 2026 revenue would reach 100.5 percent of 2025 and spending 105.8 percent, with funds for the cultural sector at 103.1 percent of last year's and 15.8 percent of spending going to national defence.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions on the state
points: US Executive Order 13722 of 15 March 2016 blocks property in US jurisdiction of the Government of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea; section 9 defines the Government as the DPRK government and its agencies, instrumentalities and controlled entities (Federal Register, 18 March 2016).

details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum is the North Korean state's. The weak point is the sanctions basis under Executive Order 13722. The sources disagree on whether the move to its present district was in 1963 or 1974; Koryo Tours, Lonely Planet and KCNA date the new building to 2013.

name: Nasjonalmuseet (National Museum of Norway)
funding: State-funded foundation; 2024 income NOK 1,059M, gifts NOK 12.5M. Fredriksen Family Art Company lends its collection on a ten-year deal and funds four PhDs. AKO Foundation and Sparebankstiftelsen DNB give.
watch: June 2022 appeal urged ending the Fredriksen deal; critics cite Seadrill's 2014 Rosneft contract. The museum sees no reason for review.
why_flagged: State-funded foundation; 2024 income NOK 1,059M, gifts NOK 12.5M. Fredriksen Family Art Company lends its collection on a ten-year deal and funds four PhDs. AKO Foundation and Sparebankstiftelsen DNB give.
records_note: Annual reports run from 2003 to 2025, accounts are filed in the Norwegian register, partners are named without a date, and the board is listed.
finances_note: FY2025 income NOK 1,084.7M: about 90 percent public grants (mostly Ministry of Culture), under 1 percent partner grants and gifts, 10 percent earned (tickets, shop, other) (accounts 2025, p. 2).
affiliations_note: Holds the Fredriksen Family Collection on long-term loan, partners with the University of Oslo on doctoral fellowships, and runs the architecture museum and Villa Stenersen.

overview: Norway's national museum of art, architecture and design, at Brynjulf Bulls plass 3 on the Vestbanen site in central Oslo (museum site; Wikipedia).

Created on 28 April 2003 by merging the National Gallery, the Museum of Contemporary Art, the Museum of Architecture and two design museums. It is state-owned and managed by the Ministry of Culture (Wikipedia).

The new building opened in June 2022. Kleihues + Schuwerk won the international architecture competition in November 2010. The government presented the project on 22 March 2013 at about NOK 5.3 billion (Wikipedia).
Holds over 400,000 works, including the first version of Edvard Munch's "The Scream" (1893) (Wikipedia).

Wikipedia says critics widely derided the building as resembling a prison, quoting the phrase "national prison". It also says the first director, Sune Nordgren, resigned in 2006 after a long period of professional criticism and staff conflicts.
The director is Ingrid Røynesdal, appointed in 2023, after Karin Hindsbo (2017 to 2023) (Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: Nasjonalmuseet: mainly public: a state-owned foundation, with private partners including the Fredriksen family
funding: The museum lists six partners: AKO Foundation, the Fredriksen Family Collection, Lise M Stolt-Nielsen and family, Sparebankstiftelsen DNB, Stiftelsen Scheibler and Viking.

Fredriksen Family Art Company: lends the Fredriksen Family Collection on a long-term basis, initial term ten years, confirmed in 2017; funds a doctoral programme with four fellowships planned for 2023 to 2027, and a separate doctoral project on Frida Hansen. Cecilie and Kathrine Fredriksen, daughters of the shipping magnate John Fredriksen, announced the partnership in 2019 and have lent more than 100 works (Apollo, 2025).

red_flags.heading: Protest against the Fredriksen partnership
points: 12 March 2022: Jeremie McGowan, former director of Nordnorsk Kunstmuseum, wrote in Klassekampen that Seadrill, "Fredriksen's drilling company", entered a major agreement with Rosneft shortly before Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, and called the museum "naive or complicit". Ruben Steinum, chair of the Association of Norwegian Visual Artists, said the public needs to know how the museum assesses partners whose wealth was partly accumulated in areas of conflict and war (Kunstkritikk, Live Drønen, 18 March 2022).

18 March 2022: communications director Eirik Kydland told Kunstkritikk the museum had seen no new circumstances that call for review, that no Fredriksen company had been affected by sanctions, and that the money comes from legitimate business operations. Director Karin Hindsbo did not respond.

10 June 2022: artists Nikhil Vettukattil, Knut Asdam, Kajsa Dahlberg and Sille Storihle launched an appeal, "A Gift we can Afford to Refuse", calling for the agreement to be terminated; it had well over 100 signatures when Kunstkritikk reported it (Tiril Flom, 10 June 2022).

The appeal argues the deal gives one powerful family too much influence, calls it an attempt to improve a company's reputation through art sponsorship, and cites John Fredriksen's business dealings from Iran to Russia, including Russia's Order of Friendship awarded in 2015 (Kunstkritikk, Flom).

press.overall: Two Kunstkritikk pieces from March and June 2022 criticise the Fredriksen deal; no criticism found of the other partners.

items.title: Live Drønen, "The National Museum of Norway Linked to Russia" (18 March 2022)
points: The partnership needs fresh scrutiny after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, given the family's links to Russia.
Names McGowan, Seadrill, Rosneft and Fredriksen; director Karin Hindsbo did not respond, communications director Eirik Kydland did.

items.title: Tiril Flom, "Artists Fight Sponsorship Agreement" (10 June 2022)
points: Reports the appeal's question whether public trust and professional integrity should outweigh the financial benefit; Åsdam is quoted as saying it "kills the professional integrity of a national public institution".
Cites as precedents that the Astrup Fearnley Museum cut ties with Lundin Oil and that the Met and the Serpentine ended Sackler sponsorship.

details.bottom_line: Nasjonalmuseet is mostly state-funded, with a named private partner, the Fredriksen family, whose loan and doctoral funding come from a shipping and drilling fortune. The weak points are the artists' 2022 appeal, the Russia links raised by McGowan. Worth watching: whether the Fredriksen agreement is renewed when its ten-year term ends.

name: Sámi Center for Contemporary Art (Sámi Dáiddaguovddáš)
funding: 2025 revenue NOK 7.9M; Sámi Parliament direct grant NOK 6.09M (2025). Finnmark county, Troms county and Arts Council Norway are shown as funders on its site.
watch: Sámi contemporary art centre, founded 1986, a foundation since 2013. The director and several board members changed over 2025-26.
records_note: Audited accounts for 2023 to 2025 are in Norway's accounts register; the site lists the full board but no annual reports or funders.
finances_note: FY2025 operating revenue NOK 7.92M against operating costs of NOK 8.15M; the register shows no grant breakdown, so the public share is not stated (Brønnøysund accounts register).
affiliations_note: Member of Kunstsentrene i Norge, the national association of 15 regional art centres.

overview: Sámi contemporary art centre at Suomageaidnu 14, Karasjok. It calls itself the leading international center for contemporary Sámi artists, with a main focus on international Sámi contemporary art with local anchoring in Sápmi (stated by the centre).

Established in 1986 (stated by the centre). The Stiftelsen Sámi Dáiddaguovddáš foundation was established on 23 August 2013 and registered on 9 January 2014 (Proff, from the Norwegian business register).

Its purpose, in its own words, is supporting, communicating and visualizing Sámi contemporary art in Europe, to indigenous areas and to the largest art arenas in the world, while providing room for new and experimental artistic practices.
A gallery shop sells books, art, handicrafts, jewellery, gifts and Sámi music.
Free entry for everyone. Open Thursday and Friday 10:00 to 16:00, Saturday and Sunday 11:00 to 16:00.

Board per the centre's website: chair Geir Tore Holm (appointed by SDS). Deputy chair Maja Kristine Jåma and deputy Piera Heaika Muotka (appointed by the Sámi Parliament). Member Svein Atle Somby and deputy Mathis Nilsen Eira (appointed by Karasjok Municipality). Two further members and two further deputies appointed by SDS.

In May 2025 the board appointed Line Kalak, a lawyer and former assistant professor of law at the Sámi University of Applied Sciences, as managing director, "the very first Sámi leader of the institution since SDG was transformed into a foundation over ten years ago" (press release, 13 May 2025). The board appointed Marija Griniuk as director for a four-year term, due to start on 25 July 2022 (centre's announcement, 19 May 2022).
details.funding_verdict: Sámi Dáiddaguovddáš (Karasjok): Sámi Parliament project funding, with board seats held by the Sámi Parliament and Karasjok Municipality
funding: The Sámi Parliament (Sametinget) funded the centre's participation at the ArtVilnius art fair in Lithuania, 4 to 6 October 2024 (stated by the centre).
Operating revenue for 2025 was NOK 7,921 thousand, with an operating result of minus NOK 229 thousand, total assets of NOK 2,051 thousand and equity of NOK 1,611 thousand at December 2025 (Proff).
details.bottom_line: The documented money behind the centre, a Sámi foundation, is the Sámi Parliament's funding of its ArtVilnius 2024 participation. The Sámi Parliament and Karasjok Municipality also appoint board members. Proff reports 2025 revenue of NOK 7.9 million.

name: UKS (Unge Kunstneres Samfund / Young Artists' Society)
funding: The Ministry of Culture is its principal funder.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
highlight: UKS is an Oslo-based institution for contemporary art and a Norwegian membership organization, founded by artists for artists in 1921.

overview: Membership organisation for professional artists and an exhibition space for contemporary art at Keysers gate 1 in Oslo, at Tullinløkka (UKS website, Store norske leksikon).
Founded by artists in 1921. It has run its own exhibition venue in Oslo since 1937 (UKS website).
Joining UKS includes membership in the Norwegian Association of Visual Artists (NBK). In 2024 UKS had about 700 members and was the largest basic organisation within NBK (Store norske leksikon).
Exhibitions are chosen by working artists on the board and the director, with the programme drawn from an annual open call (UKS website).

Besides exhibitions it holds artist talks and public events and administers artist grants and residency places (Store norske leksikon), and it does political work through consultations and hearings. Its main projects are climate and sustainability, Palestine, the studio situation and the report on artists' living conditions (UKS website).
Governed by a chair and six board members elected for two-year terms by the annual general assembly. The current chair is Ragnhild Aamås (UKS website).
Its archive of nearly 100 years is held by the Riksarkivet in Oslo (Store norske leksikon).
Visiting: during exhibition periods open Wednesday 12 to 17, Thursday 12 to 19, Friday to Sunday 12 to 17. There is no entrance fee (UKS website).
details.funding_verdict: UKS: mainly public: the Norwegian Ministry of Culture
funding: UKS describes itself as a non-profit organisation with the Ministry of Culture as its principal funder (UKS website).
Store norske leksikon states it is mainly financed by the Ministry of Culture and Equality.
details.bottom_line: UKS is an artist-run membership organisation financed mainly by the Norwegian Ministry of Culture, with a published board elected by its members.

name: Oman Across Ages Museum
funding: The pages read did not name a funder or cost. The National (13 March 2023) said it was established under royal orders of the late Sultan Qaboos bin Said and inaugurated by Sultan Haitham bin Tarik.
watch: A national history museum on a 300,000 square metre site in Manah, opened on 13 March 2023 by Sultan Haitham, its foundation stone laid by Sultan Qaboos on 14 July 2015. No funder was named in the pages read.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: A museum on 300,000 square metres in Manah, Al Dakhiliyah, with about 66,591 square metres of building designed to resemble mountains (The National, 13 March 2023).
Established by royal orders of Sultan Qaboos, who laid the foundation stone on 14 July 2015; Sultan Haitham bin Tarik opened it on 13 March 2023 (The National, 13 March 2023).

What is there: a mammoth jaw about 35 million years old from Dhofar, a 250-million-year-old trilobite fauna fossil from Mahut, a replica Majan reed ship, 200 interactive screens and map projection (The National, 13 March 2023).
Archive: the pages read did not describe an archive or library.
details.funding_verdict: Oman Across Ages Museum: state project under royal orders; no amounts found.
funding: Established under royal orders of Sultan Qaboos (The National, 13 March 2023).
No reporting found, in the pages read, of cost, contractors or operating budget.
details.bottom_line: A royal-ordered national museum; the pages read give no cost or operator beyond the sultans.

name: Royal Opera House Muscat
funding: The pages read did not state how the house is funded. Arab News said Sultan Qaboos bin Said Al Said ordered Oman's first opera house in 2001.
watch: A 1,100-seat opera house designed by WATG, ordered by Sultan Qaboos in 2001 and opened in October 2011 with Puccini's Turandot. The pages read did not name its owner or funders.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: A 1,100-seat opera house with a flexible stage that can take an orchestra pit, in Muscat (Arab News).
Sultan Qaboos bin Said Al Said ordered Oman's first opera house in 2001; it opened in October 2011 with Puccini's Turandot, designed by WATG (Arab News).
What is there: the house stages opera, orchestral and other performance; no company or repertoire list was read.
Archive: the pages read did not describe an archive.
details.funding_verdict: Royal Opera House Muscat: ordered by the Sultan; no financing found.
funding: Sultan Qaboos ordered the project in 2001 (Arab News); the article said budget constraints were set aside in favour of luxury but gave no amount.
No reporting found, in the pages read, of operating budget, ticket income or sponsors.
details.bottom_line: The royal origin is documented; the money today is not in the pages read. Check Omani government and ROHM filings.

name: Centro Cultural de la República El Cabildo
funding: Cultural arm of Paraguay's National Congress, paid from the congressional budget (a G. 1.88 billion extension for a new building in 2025). Entry to the ground-floor rooms is free.
watch: Shows mid-20th-century to present Paraguayan art, including Olga Blinder and Livio Abramo. A December 2020 fire hit the newer block; the heritage building was safe.
records_note: Its site has programme and news pages only; its parent is the Paraguayan Congress.

overview: Cultural centre of the Paraguayan National Congress in the former Cabildo (town council) building on Avenida de la República, Asunción (Última Hora, 2021).

Opened on 14 May 2004 (English Wikipedia says 14 March) at the initiative of Carlos Mateo Balmelli, then president of Congress, with Chilean president Ricardo Lagos and the writer Augusto Roa Bastos present. Margarita Morselli was director general (ABC Color, 2019). Morselli led it for 20 years until Aníbal Saucedo Rodas replaced her in July 2024 (La Nación).

The building's refit and current design date from the government of Carlos Antonio López, with the Spanish architect Pascual Urdapilleta linked to the design. Spanish Wikipedia gives 1857 as the inauguration. It housed the executive until 1894 and Congress until 2003 (Spanish and English Wikipedia).
On site: the Sala del Barro, the Sala de Arte Sacro, museum rooms for the Cabildo, music and film, the Augusto Roa Bastos library and two temporary exhibition rooms (Spanish Wikipedia).

A fire on the night before 25 December 2020 destroyed the Congress Symphony Orchestra's rehearsal hall and other rooms in the newer block. The heritage building and museum halls were not affected (Última Hora, 25 December 2020). It reopened to the public in May 2023 (Wikipedia).
Visiting: in February 2021 the ground-floor spaces were free and the temporary exhibition rooms were open Monday to Friday 8am to 1pm (Última Hora).
details.funding_verdict: Centro Cultural de la República El Cabildo: public: the Paraguayan National Congress's budget
funding: It depends on the National Congress (Última Hora, 2021). Its director Saucedo Rodas said in July 2024 that its budget was 31,000 million guaraníes, shared with the Congress's Central Library and Archive (La Nación, 12 July 2024). The Senate head Basilio Núñez called the budget the main obstacle (La Nación).

In July 2025 Decree 4309 raised Congress's budget by G. 4,280 million, of which G. 1,880 million is for repairing and extending El Cabildo, funded by an external loan (Última Hora, 30 July 2025). La Nación described the G. 1,880 million as a budget expansion authorised by the decree and does not mention a loan; it reported the sum for a two-storey building with a rehearsal room, exhibition room and heritage store next to the Casa Bicentenario de la Música (La Nación, 1 August 2025).

press.overall: Little criticism, and none in art magazines. Two Última Hora pieces criticise the centre's cultural policy and a Congress spending decree that includes it.

items.title: unsigned, "Artistas piden a Lugo la destitución de Margarita Morselli" (2017)
points: A manifesto signed by 300 artists and cultural activists asked Congress president Fernando Lugo to remove Morselli. The artist Ricardo de la Vega spoke for the group.
They argued that cultural policy should be popular and reach the whole population, not a select group in Asunción, and that neighbourhoods such as the Chacarita had been sidelined for years.
They called the hiring of the foreign group Il Divo for the 2011 bicentennial, with thousands of local artists left out, a very serious mistake. The piece carries no reply from Morselli.

items.title: Redacción ÚH, "Congreso tiene luz verde para gastar en construir un obelisco" (2025)
points: Calls the Decree 4309 spending, including the G. 1,880 million for El Cabildo, "un despilfarro impropio de un país en crisis" (translation: a waste unfit for a country in crisis), and says Congress presidents acquired buildings to house political allies, using art and culture as cover.
Names no problem with El Cabildo's programme; the criticism targets Congress.

wider_context: Última Hora says Congress has seven other premises besides its main building, costing over G. 118,880 million by the Senate's own inventory, and criticises an official car park and a "quincho de oro" in the inner courtyard.
El Cabildo depends on Congress (Última Hora, 2021), and its extension is paid from the decree the article criticises.
details.bottom_line: The money behind the centre is the Congress budget, with a 2025 extension added by an executive decree; no private funder or flagged industry was found. The weak points are that no accounts or governance are published, that the sources differ on whether a loan pays for the extension, and that the extension is part of a spending decree Última Hora called a waste. Watch the construction of the new block.
